study.title: Ezekiel 47 - the river of the sanctuary and the shared heritage
study.overview: This chapter unites two central images: a river that is born from the temple and leads to life where it passes, and the distribution of the land in inheritance to the tribes and also to the foreigners who inhabit them. In verses 1 to 12, the vision shows that the presence of God, coming out of the sanctuary, grows surprisingly and turns dead waters into living waters, with fish, fruit trees and healing. In verses 13 to 20, the Lord reaffirms the promise of the earth and sets its limits with language of inheritance and order. In verses 21 to 23, the distribution includes the resident foreigners, indicating that participation in the inheritance is not restricted to birth, but reaches those who join the people in the midst of the tribes.

outline.title: The river that comes out of the temple and generates life
outline.explanation: Ezekiel sees waters that come out of the sanctuary, start small and become a river impossible to cross on foot. As they advance, they make the waters of the sea healthy, produce many fish and grow fruit trees whose leaves serve as medicine. The image communicates expansion, healing, and fruitfulness from the presence of God.

outline.title: The promised land is redefined as an ordered inheritance
outline.explanation: The Lord declares the limits of the land which shall be divided among the twelve tribes, with Joseph receiving two parts. The emphasis is not only on geography, but on God's faithfulness to the oath made to the parents and the organization of the life of the people before the promise.

outline.title: The foreigner also receives inheritance
outline.explanation: The land must be drawn to Israel and also to the foreigners who live among the people and have children there. They are treated as natives and receive inheritance in the tribe where they live, showing that land sharing includes real welcome and integration.

study.context: The chapter closes Ezekiel's vision with two parts connected to the sanctuary and the earth. The text presents the temple as a center of life and the earth as a gift promised by oath. The notes highlight that the distribution of the land, at the end of the book, is treated as theology in the form of geography: space, access and position in relation to the temple matter. They also note that the inclusion of foreigners in the inheritance is a striking point of the final section.
study.theology: The main theological message is that life flows from the presence of God and not from human effort. The river begins small, but it grows until it becomes uncontrollable, a sign that divine action does not depend on grandiose beginnings. The waters heal, multiply life and make fertile what was once sterile, which points to integral restoration. In the second half of the chapter, the promised land reaffirms God's faithfulness to his covenant: what has been sworn to the fathers will be fulfilled. At the same time, the inheritance is not presented as a closed privilege in ethnicity or origin, because foreign residents receive real participation. In evangelical reading, many see in this an announcement of God's grace that reaches beyond the borders of Israel; however, this should be read as an interpretation of the meaning of the text, not as an explicit statement that the chapter already describes in detail the later church.

scholarViews.insight: The river symbolizes the transforming range of God's restored presence: what is born in the temple spreads and brings life around, rather than death.
Vision has a spiritual sense and mystery; God's oath to parents ensures that the promised inheritance has not been forgotten, despite the time of discontinuity.
The inclusion of foreigners in the division of the earth is understood as a sign of the extension of blessings also to the Gentiles, in Christian reading of the text.

questions: What does the image of the river teach about how God's presence transforms places of death into places of life?
How does the promise of the earth confront the tendency to think that time annulled the oath of God?
How does the inclusion of foreigners challenge the community of faith to practice real acceptance and sharing?
study.practice: Take this chapter to prayer by asking God to make his life flow from his service, his home and his community. Also ask where there are "salgada" or stagnates" areas that need God's healing, and practice concrete hospitality: welcome, include and recognize outsiders as participants in community life. Finally, remember that God's faithfulness to what he promised sustains hope even when reality seems delayed.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is strongly symbolic, and the notes presented bring interpretive readings that do not always agree with each other. It is not safe to state, only from these sources, all historical details or the exact application of each measure and border. There are also differences between commentators about how much the view should be read literally, spiritually or kindly.
